basic.title: Basic Chemistry
basic.overview: This route introduces the first families of compounds: water, carbon oxides, ammonia, salts, and simple metal or sulfur oxides.

levels.theory: Water is one of the first stable molecules students meet. It shows how two hydrogens can connect around one oxygen to form a simple but essential structure.
levels.mechanicSummary: Place atoms on the board, connect them with single bonds, and match the target molecule pattern.

levels.theory: Carbon and oxygen can join in different ratios. This lesson introduces the smallest carbon oxide and teaches that the same elements can build different substances.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use the same board-building mechanic, but now compare how one carbon behaves when combined with oxygen.

levels.theory: Carbon dioxide extends the previous idea by adding another oxygen. It helps learners notice how changing atom counts changes the final compound and its structure.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build the next carbon oxide by arranging one carbon with two oxygen atoms in the correct connection pattern.

levels.theory: Ammonia introduces nitrogen as a central atom that can connect to several hydrogens. It is a good first example of a different central-node pattern.
levels.mechanicSummary: Choose the coefficients that make nitrogen and hydrogen atom counts match before ammonia is formed.

levels.theory: Methane is one of the simplest carbon-based molecules. It shows carbon as a strong central builder that can connect to multiple hydrogens.
levels.mechanicSummary: Practice a hub-style structure where one carbon becomes the main anchor for the full molecule.

levels.theory: Hydrochloric acid introduces chlorine as a halogen partner. This lesson expands the route from water and oxides into acid-like combinations.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use a simpler two-atom pattern and learn how a new element changes the chemistry route.

levels.theory: Salt is one of the most recognizable compounds in beginner chemistry. It introduces the idea of metal and nonmetal combinations in a very familiar form.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a basic metal-nonmetal pair and compare it with the acid lesson before it.

levels.theory: Calcium oxide moves the route into basic metal oxides. It helps learners compare how oxygen combines with a different type of element.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance calcium reacting with oxygen so both sides conserve every atom.

levels.theory: Iron oxide lessons introduce transition metals in a simplified form. This first step starts with the smaller oxide before moving to a more complex iron compound.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a compact oxide structure and prepare for a larger iron pattern in the next lesson.

levels.theory: Iron(III) oxide scales the same family into a larger structure. It shows that one chemistry topic can expand into more complex patterns without changing the mechanic.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use the same connection mechanic, but manage a denser structure with more atoms on the board.

levels.theory: Sulfur dioxide introduces sulfur oxides and reactive gas compounds. It is the first step in a small sulfur branch of the route.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a sulfur-centered structure and compare it with earlier oxygen-based compounds.

levels.theory: Sulfur trioxide extends the sulfur branch and closes the basic route with a larger oxide. It reinforces the idea that one topic can develop across multiple lessons.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance sulfur dioxide turning into sulfur trioxide as the route's final oxide checkpoint.

acids-bases.title: Acids, Bases, and pH
acids-bases.overview: This route starts from neutral water, splits into acid and base branches, and then reconnects them through familiar school-level neutralization ideas.

levels.theory: Water is the natural baseline for acid-base chemistry. It gives the route a neutral starting point before stronger acids and bases begin to branch away.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build the neutral reference molecule first so later acid and base patterns have something to compare against.

levels.theory: Hydrochloric acid is a classic strong acid in school chemistry. It is a simple first step into the acid branch because the formula is compact and easy to recognize.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use a short two-atom build to open the acid side of the route.

levels.theory: Sodium hydroxide is a classic strong base. It gives the route a clean comparison against the acid branch while still using a small formula.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a simple hydroxide pattern and compare it with the acid lesson beside it.

levels.theory: Hypochlorous acid shows how adding oxygen can change the behavior and identity of a chlorine-based acid. It pushes the acid branch into a larger pattern.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance chlorine reacting with water to produce hydrochloric and hypochlorous acids.

levels.theory: Carbonic acid forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water. It is a good school example of how gases, solutions, and acidity can connect.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a larger oxygen-rich acid and notice how the structure becomes more branch-like.

levels.theory: Potassium hydroxide extends the same base family as sodium hydroxide. It helps learners compare how similar hydroxides can swap the metal while keeping the main pattern.
levels.mechanicSummary: Reuse the hydroxide idea with a new metal to reinforce the pattern.

levels.theory: Ammonia introduces a base that is not a metal hydroxide. It broadens the route and shows that base behavior is not limited to one kind of formula.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a nitrogen-centered base pattern and compare it with the hydroxides.

levels.theory: Nitric acid expands the acid branch into a nitrogen-oxygen framework. It is a strong example of how oxygen-rich acids create larger connection patterns.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance the oxygen-rich formation of nitric acid by matching N, H, and O counts.

levels.theory: Sulfurous acid connects sulfur chemistry with acidity. It gives the learner another oxygen-rich acid family to compare against carbonic and nitric acids.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a sulfur-centered acid structure with multiple oxygen branches.

levels.theory: Calcium hydroxide scales the base branch into a bigger hydroxide with two OH groups. It helps learners notice repeated groups inside one compound.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use one central metal with two hydroxide branches to make a larger base structure.

levels.theory: Magnesium hydroxide keeps the same overall base idea but swaps the center metal. It reinforces comparison inside one chemistry family.
levels.mechanicSummary: Repeat the two-branch hydroxide pattern with a different metal center.

levels.theory: Sodium chloride closes the route with a familiar salt. It acts as a simple endpoint after spending the route comparing acids, bases, and their patterns.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance a neutralization equation where acid and base produce salt and water.

salts-oxides.title: Salts and Oxides
salts-oxides.overview: This route compares salt families and oxide families side by side, then expands into sulfur and iron examples so the learner sees how broad inorganic chemistry can become.

levels.theory: Sodium chloride is the classic school example of a salt. It gives the route a familiar start before the player branches into more varied salts and oxides.
levels.mechanicSummary: Begin with the simplest familiar salt so the rest of the route has a strong comparison point.

levels.theory: Potassium chloride helps learners compare one simple chloride salt with another. The main structure stays compact while the metal changes.
levels.mechanicSummary: Swap one metal for another and notice how the salt family pattern stays recognizable.

levels.theory: Sodium oxide opens the oxide branch. It shows that the same metal can form a very different compound once oxygen replaces chlorine.
levels.mechanicSummary: Start the oxide side of the route with a small but reactive sodium compound.

levels.theory: Calcium chloride expands the salt branch into a larger pattern. It helps learners notice that one metal can pair with more than one nonmetal atom.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a three-atom salt where the center metal connects to two matching halogens.

levels.theory: Magnesium chloride gives another comparison inside the same chloride family. It reinforces how salts can repeat a structural idea while changing the center metal.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance magnesium reacting with chlorine to form a chloride salt.

levels.theory: Calcium oxide is one of the classic school oxides and an important material in industry. It helps the route shift into stronger metal-oxygen comparisons.
levels.mechanicSummary: Keep the mechanic simple while moving the oxide branch to a new metal.

levels.theory: Magnesium oxide keeps the oxide branch compact and comparable. It reinforces that metal oxides form a clear family with related but distinct compounds.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build another small metal oxide and compare it directly with calcium oxide.

levels.theory: Sodium sulfide expands the route beyond chlorides and introduces sulfur as the nonmetal partner in a salt. This broadens the salt family without changing the overall lesson structure.
levels.mechanicSummary: Use a compact sulfur-centered salt to show that salts are more than just metal chlorides.

levels.theory: Potassium oxide compares directly with sodium oxide. It helps the learner see a repeating oxide idea inside the alkali metals.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build another alkali-metal oxide and compare how familiar the pattern already feels.

levels.theory: Sodium peroxide shows that adding one more oxygen can create a noticeably different compound family. It gives the oxide route more depth than a simple one-oxygen pattern.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance sodium peroxide formation and compare the atom ratio with simpler oxides.

levels.theory: Iron(III) chloride brings a transition metal into the salt branch. It is a useful bridge from simple salts toward denser inorganic structures.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a larger chloride salt with one central iron and three surrounding chlorine atoms.

levels.theory: Iron(II) oxide starts the iron oxide family in a compact form. It prepares the learner for a more complex iron oxide later in the route.
levels.mechanicSummary: Introduce iron into the oxide branch with the smaller oxide first.

levels.theory: Calcium sulfide continues the sulfur-salt branch with a different metal. It strengthens comparison across the salt family without changing the overall mechanic.
levels.mechanicSummary: Build a compact sulfur salt and compare it with sodium sulfide.

levels.theory: Sulfur dioxide expands the oxide branch from metal oxides into nonmetal oxides. It shows that oxide chemistry includes gases and reactive molecular compounds too.
levels.mechanicSummary: Shift into sulfur-centered oxide chemistry while keeping the same bond-building mechanic.

levels.theory: Iron(III) oxide expands the iron branch into a denser pattern. It demonstrates how one oxide family can grow in complexity without changing the theme.
levels.mechanicSummary: Return to iron and build the larger oxide pattern after the simpler FeO step.

levels.theory: Sulfur trioxide closes the route with a larger sulfur oxide. It works as a final capstone because it combines a familiar center atom with a more advanced oxygen-rich arrangement.
levels.mechanicSummary: Balance the final sulfur oxide equation before closing the salts-and-oxides route.
